formulations.note: No hydrochlorothiazide-only product was found on emc; the UK SPC used is from MHRA Products. The 25 mg tablet is scored and can be divided into equal doses.

src.q: Each tablet contains 25 mg of hydrochlorothiazide
The tablet can be divided into equal doses.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Adults: oedema of cardiac or renal origin; oedema of hepatic origin (usually with a potassium-sparing diuretic); arterial hypertension.

src.q: Oedemas of cardiac or renal origin. Oedemas of hepatic origin, usually in combination with a potassium-sparing diuretic. Arterial hypertension.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions stated in the UK SPC.

items.t: 12.5 or 25 mg daily (single dose or two divided doses, with or without food). Full effect in 3-4 weeks. If 25 mg/day is not enough, add another antihypertensive rather than increasing the dose.

src.q: The doses currently recommended in arterial hypertension are 12.5 or 25 mg/day.
If blood pressure is not sufficiently lowered with a dose of 25 mg/day, combined treatment with another antihypertensive drug is recommended.
For a given dose, the maximum effect is achieved within 3 to 4 weeks.
The daily dose of Hydrochlorothiazide can be given as a single dose or divided over two doses, with or without food.

items.t: Start 50-100 mg/day (possibly 200 mg/day); titrate to the lowest effective dose for limited periods. Maintenance 25-50 mg daily or on alternate days.

src.q: The starting dose is 50 to 100 mg/day, possibly 200 mg/day.
The maintenance dose is 25 mg to 50 mg/day or every other day.
The lowest effective dose should be identified by titration and only administered for limited periods.

items.t: Correct sodium and/or volume depletion before combining with an ACE inhibitor, angiotensin II antagonist or direct renin inhibitor; otherwise start under close medical supervision. After long-term use, withdraw gradually.

src.q: Sodium depletion and / or volume must be corrected before using hydrochlorothiazide in combination with an ACE inhibitor, an antagonist of angiotensin II or a direct renin inhibitor.
After long-term treatment, therapy with hydrochlorothiazide should be discontinued gradually.
Otherwise, treatment should be initiated under close medical supervision.

items.t: Elderly: take possible reduced renal function into account.

src.q: In the treatment of elderly patients, attention should be paid to possible restrictions to renal function.

items.t: No experience in children and adolescents; should not be used.

src.q: There is no experience in children and adolescents. Therefore, hydrochlorothiazide should not be used in children and adolescents.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to hydrochlorothiazide or any excipient; anuria; severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min).

src.q: Hypersensitivity to hydrochlorothiazide or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Anuria. Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min).

items.t: Generally not recommended with bilateral renal artery stenosis, a single functioning kidney, or hypokalaemia.

src.q: Hydrochlorothiazide is generally not recommended in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis or a single functioning kidney or with hypokalaemia.

items.t: Non-melanoma skin cancer (basal and squamous cell): risk rises with cumulative dose. Tell patients the risk, advise regular skin checks and sun/UV protection; examine suspicious lesions; reconsider use after previous skin cancer (SPC and MHRA).

src.q: An increased risk of non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC) [basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)] with increasing cumulative dose of hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) exposure has been observed
reconsider the use of hydrochlorothiazide in patients who have had previous skin cancer
Suspicious skin lesions should be promptly examined

items.t: Electrolytes: hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia (major arrhythmia risk with long QT, heart disease, digitalis). Start only after correcting hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, and after normalising sodium/volume depletion.

src.q: Treatment with thiazide diuretics should only be started after correction of hypokalaemia and concurrently occurring existing hypomagnesemia.
Thiazides should be only used after normalization of any existing sodium and / or volume depletion.

items.t: Hypercalcaemia: use with caution and only after correction; stop if hypercalcaemia develops. Stop before parathyroid function tests.

src.q: Hydrochlorothiazide should be used with caution in patients with hypercalcemia and should be administered only after correction of any pre- existing hypercalcemia.
Hydrochlorothiazide should be discontinued if hypercalcemia occurs during treatment.
Thiazides should be discontinued before carrying out parathyroid function tests.

items.t: Severe liver damage: use with caution (electrolyte imbalance, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome in cirrhotic ascites).

src.q: Thiazides, like other diuretics may induce electrolyte imbalance, hepatic encephalopathy or hepatorenal syndrome when used to treat cirrhotic ascites.
Hydrochlorothiazide should be used with caution particularly in patients with severe liver damage.

items.t: Uric acid may rise and trigger gout; glucose tolerance may fall and lipids rise (antidiabetic dose changes may be needed).

src.q: This can trigger attacks of gout in susceptible patients.
In diabetic patient dosage adjustments of insulin or oral hypoglycaemic agents may be required.

items.t: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (very rare): withdraw if suspected; do not give again to anyone who had ARDS after hydrochlorothiazide.

src.q: If diagnosis of ARDS is suspected, Hydrochlorothiazide should be withdrawn and appropriate treatment given.
Hydrochlorothiazide should not be administered to patients who previously experienced ARDS following hydrochlorothiazide intake.

items.t: Choroidal effusion, acute myopia and acute angle-closure glaucoma: stop as soon as possible. Risk factors include sulphonamide or penicillin allergy.

src.q: The primary treatment is to discontinue hydrochlorothiazide as soon as possible.
Risk factors for developing acute angle-closure glaucoma include a history of sulphonamide or penicillin allergy.

items.t: Systemic lupus erythematosus may be exacerbated or activated. Photosensitivity: stop treatment if it occurs.

src.q: exacerbation or activation of systemic lupus erythematosus has been reported with thiazide diuretics, including hydrochlorothiazide.
If a photosensitivity reaction occurs treatment should be discontinued.

items.t: Sulfonamide: cross-reactivity with sulfonamide antibacterials is theoretical and not clinically confirmed (SPC); SPS also states it is not expected.

src.q: The possibility of cross-reactivity especially with other antibacterials including sulfonamides is theoretical and not clinically confirmed.
Cross-reactivity between antibiotic and non-antibiotic sulfonamides is not expected, including in people who had a life-threatening reaction to a sulfonamide.

items.t: Lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption syndrome should not take this medicine.

items.t: Lithium: not recommended (raised lithium, toxicity). If essential, monitor lithium closely and adjust its dose.

src.q: Concomitant use not recommended: Lithium: Increased serum lithium levels with signs of lithium overdose
If this combination proves essential, serum lithium levels should be closely monitored and the lithium dose should be adjusted.

items.t: Medicines that may cause torsades de pointes (e.g. amiodarone, sotalol, citalopram, escitalopram, domperidone, erythromycin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, haloperidol, methadone): correct hypokalaemia first; clinical, electrolyte and ECG monitoring.

src.q: Increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias, especially torsades de pointes. Correct any hypokalaemia before administering the medicine and perform clinical, electrolyte and electrocardiographic monitoring.

items.t: NSAIDs, and aspirin at analgesic/antipyretic doses (500 mg or more per dose) or anti-inflammatory doses (1 g or more per dose and/or 3 g or more daily): acute renal failure in at-risk (elderly/dehydrated) patients and reduced antihypertensive effect. Hydrate and monitor renal function at the start.

src.q: Acute renal failure in at risk patients (elderly and / or dehydrated)
For anti-inflammatory doses of acetylsalicylic acid (≥1 g per dose and / or ≥3 g daily) or for analgesic or antipyretic doses (≥500 mg per dose and / or <3 g per day)
Hydrate the patient and monitor renal function at start of treatment.

items.t: Hyponatraemia risk adds up with other diuretics, desmopressin, SSRIs, carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine. Carbamazepine: monitor; if possible use another class of diuretic.

src.q: These are diuretics, desmopressin, serotonin reuptake inhibiting antidepressants, carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine. The combination of these drugs increase the risk of hyponatremia.
Carbamazepine Risk of symptomatic hyponatraemia. Clinical and biological monitoring. If possible, use another class of diuretic.

items.t: ACE inhibitors / angiotensin II antagonists: sudden hypotension and/or acute renal failure if sodium-depleted. Stop the diuretic first or start at a low dose; monitor creatinine in the first weeks.

src.q: Risk of sudden hypotension and / or acute renal failure when starting or increasing the dose of an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin II antagonist when there is pre-existing sodium depletion.
renal function (serum creatinine) should be monitored during the first weeks of treatment with ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II antagonists.

items.t: Other potassium-lowering medicines (loop diuretics, stimulant laxatives, glucocorticoids): more hypokalaemia; monitor and correct potassium. Potassium-sparing diuretics: hypo- or hyperkalaemia possible; monitor potassium.

src.q: These are potassium lowering diuretics, alone or combined; stimulant laxatives; glucocorticoids
Monitor serum potassium, possibly ECG and, if necessary, reconsider the treatment.

items.t: Other antihypertensives: reducing the dose is advised when combined, at least initially. Orthostatic hypotension: alpha-blockers (including tamsulosin), nitrates, PDE5 inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants. Calcium: hypercalcaemia risk. Digitalis: hypokalaemia increases its toxicity (correct potassium; clinical, electrolyte and ECG monitoring). Iodinated contrast: rehydrate first. Ciclosporin: creatinine may rise. Chelating resins: separate doses by more than 2 hours if possible.

src.q: Alpha-blockers for urological problems (alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, tamsulosin, terazosin) Hypotensive effect increased.
Especially nitrates, phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, alpha blockers for urological problems, of tricyclic antidepressants and phenothiazines
Calcium Risk of hypercalcaemia due to reduced urinary calcium excretion.
It is advised to reduce the dose when combined with other antihypertensives, at least initially.
Hypokalaemia increases the toxic effects of digitalis.
Rehydration before administration of the iodinated product.
Risk of increased creatinine without changes in ciclosporin blood levels
with an interval of more than 2 hours, if possible

src.q: Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min).
No adjustment to the starting dose is necessary in patients with mild to moderate renal impairment

items.t: SPC: insufficient data; crosses the placenta. In the 2nd and 3rd trimesters may impair fetoplacental perfusion and cause fetal/neonatal jaundice, electrolyte imbalance and thrombocytopenia. Must not be used for pregnancy oedema, hypertension or pre-eclampsia; should not be used for essential hypertension except in rare cases where no other treatment could be used.

Hydrochlorothiazide must not be used in women with pregnancy oedema, hypertension or preeclampsia
Hydrochlorothiazide should not be used for the treatment of essential hypertension in pregnant women except in rare cases where no other treatment could be used.

items.t: BUMPS (diuretics): can be used if prescribed by a doctor but rarely needed; may reduce placental blood flow (extra growth scans). For high blood pressure, a different medicine is usually offered.

src.q: A diuretic can be used in pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor.
If you take a diuretic to treat high blood pressure, you will usually be offered a different medicine that is known to be safe during pregnancy.

items.t: Not recommended: passes into milk in small amounts; high doses may inhibit milk production. If used, keep the dose as low as possible.

src.q: The use of hydrochlorothiazide during breast-feeding is not recommended. If hydrochlorothiazide is indicated, the doses should be as low as possible.

items.t: No human fertility data; no effect on fertility in animal studies.

src.q: There are no human fertility data for hydrochlorothiazide.

items.t: Very common: hypokalaemia, raised blood lipids. Common: hyperuricaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyponatraemia, orthostatic hypotension, diarrhoea, loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting, urticaria and other skin reactions, impotence.

items.t: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (very rare): dyspnoea, fever, hypotension within minutes to hours - withdraw and treat.

src.q: At the onset, symptoms include dyspnoea, fever, pulmonary deterioration and hypotension.
Pulmonary oedema typically develops within minutes to hours after hydrochlorothiazide intake.

items.t: Acute angle-closure glaucoma / choroidal effusion (not known): acute reduced vision or eye pain - stop as soon as possible.

src.q: Symptoms include an acute onset of decreased visual acuity or acute ocular pain

items.t: Non-melanoma skin cancer (not known). Rare: thrombocytopenia. Very rare: bone marrow depression, haemolytic anaemia, agranulocytosis, necrotising vasculitis, toxic epidermal necrolysis, pancreatitis. Uncommon: acute renal impairment.

src.q: Not known non-melanoma skin cancer (Basal cell carcinoma and Squamous cell carcinoma)

items.t: Potassium in the week after starting, then regularly (a check at 3-4 weeks may be considered); sodium regularly (more often in elderly, malnourished, cirrhosis); calcium regularly.
